cultivar: Si Ji Chun, Jin Xuan, Da Ye oolong or TTES #8, depending on the maker
processing: Withered leaf goes through the same nitrogen-flushed anaerobic cycles as GABA oolong, so the lot reaches at least 150 mg of GABA per 100 g, then is rolled, fully oxidised and dried; usually unroasted.
harvest_season: Any season; summer and autumn lowland leaf is the usual source.
appearance_dry: Dark reddish-black twisted strips or small balls with a sweet-sour, raisin-like smell.
appearance_wet: Soft copper-brown leaves, fully oxidised and even.
taste_profile: Raisin, prune and baked plum over a mild malty base with a gentle sour-sweet tang, rounder and less tart than GABA oolong, with a smooth, low-astringency body.

brewing.notes: Water just off the boil, three minutes Western-style or short gongfu steeps; good cold-brewed, where the fruit comes forward. Takes milk and honey without complaint.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's tea by maker, usually with the GABA content stated and often with a laboratory report, which is the thing to ask for; prices are modest and it keeps two or three years sealed. It is not graded in competitions or sold by garden.
description:
GABA black tea is the fully oxidised cousin of Taiwanese GABA oolong: the same anaerobic treatment of the fresh leaf, followed by black-tea processing instead of oolong processing. It is made in the Nantou lowlands and in Taitung, where producers around Luye have taken it up, from whichever cultivar the maker has, Si Ji Chun, Jin Xuan, Da Ye oolong or the Assam-type number 8.

The withered leaf is held in a nitrogen-flushed, oxygen-free chamber in cycles alternated with air until it meets Taiwan's threshold of 150 milligrams of GABA per 100 grams, then rolled, oxidised fully and dried. The anaerobic step gives GABA tea its distinctive sweet-sour, dried-fruit character, and full oxidation rounds it off, so the black version is softer and less tart than the oolong.

Expect raisin, prune and baked plum over a mild malty base, with a gentle tang on the finish rather than the oolong's sharper sourness, and a smooth, low-astringency body. It brews easily: water just off the boil, three minutes Western-style or short gongfu steeps, and it is good cold-brewed, where the fruit comes forward. It takes milk and honey without complaint.

It is sold as the current year's tea by maker, usually with the GABA content stated and often with a laboratory report, which is the thing to ask for; it keeps two or three years sealed. Prices are modest. Any health benefit is a marketing claim rather than a settled fact, so buy it for the flavour, which is genuinely unlike other black tea.

If you are curious about GABA tea, start here before the oolong; it is the gentler of the two.
sources_note: That Luye (Taitung) producers popularised GABA black in the 2010s is my understanding from Taiwanese trade coverage, not a documented date.
history:
The technique behind this tea comes from Japan: from 1984 researchers at the national tea institute stored fresh leaf in nitrogen and found that GABA built up in it, and later found the same in green, oolong and black tea alike. Taiwanese makers took the method up widely, and most attention has gone to GABA oolong.

The black version is a later and quieter branch of the same idea. Little is documented about who first made it in Taiwan or when.
